docs.title: Additive animation clips
docs.text:
Additive animation clips are a core tool within an animation runtime but sadly, how additive animations are blended and applied is not standard. As such, this library aims to support the most common additive modes. Contributions welcome!

The core logic for additive clips lives here.

docs.title: The transform space
docs.text:
Two independent properties tell compression how to measure the error of a clip:

  • The transform space of the clip: how a sample uses the transform hierarchy, see transform_space_t (see here). The track array holds it: set it with track_array::set_transform_space.
    • local (the default): each transform is relative to its parent transform.
    • mesh: each transform is in object space (mesh space). It does not use its parent transform. Compression measures the error of each transform alone: the error of a parent does not move its children.
    • mesh_rotation: the rotation of each transform is in object space, its translation and scale are relative to its parent transform. The rotation of a parent does not change the object rotation of its children, but the parent still moves them. Compression measures the error in object space with this rule: object = mul(local, parent_object), with local.rotation = mul(rotation, conjugate(parent_object.rotation)).
  • The base of the clip: how a sample combines with its base clip. A transform_base_desc_t (see here) holds the base format (format, see additive_clip_format8 and the formats below) and the base tracks (tracks). With none, the clip has no base. With custom, the adapter combines them, see below.

Compression first combines each sample with the base. Then it puts the result in object space to measure the error. The transform space does not change the compressed data: decompression returns the samples of the clip, and your runtime applies them to the base.

The base is always in local space, with the transform hierarchy of the clip: the transform space of the base tracks must be local. In mesh space, compression puts the base in mesh space with rtm::vqv_mul (the scale of a parent does not shear its children). Then it combines each sample with the base in mesh space. In mesh rotation space, compression puts only the rotations of the base in mesh space, then it combines each sample with the base: the rotations in mesh space, the translations and scales in local space. The compressed tracks keep the parent indices of the clip.

The mesh rotation space has two limits:

  • It needs the object rotation of each parent: it supports the vqf, vqsf, vqvf, and vqmf runtime transform types (and automatic). The product of these types multiplies the rotations as quaternions, the VQM scale/shear matrix holds the shear. It does not support matrix3x4f: a matrix mixes the rotation with the scale and the shear. It does not support a custom transform adapter: ACL cannot read its rotation.
  • It does not support the relative base format: that format multiplies the whole transforms, but the rotations and the translations are in different spaces. Use additive0 or additive1.

A rotation of a parent moves its children but does not rotate them: the subtree is not rigid with respect to the parent. Thus the bit rate search cannot cache the transform of a child relative to its parent, as it does in local space. With the vqf and vqsf types, the search caches the rotation of each child and the sum of the translations below the parent. With the vqvf and vqmf types, the search multiplies each transform chain, and compression is slower.

raw_track_list.set_transform_space(transform_space_t::mesh_rotation);

transform_base_desc_t transform_base;
transform_base.format = additive_clip_format8::additive1;
transform_base.tracks = &base_track_list;

error_result result = compress_track_list(allocator, raw_track_list, settings, transform_base, out_compressed_tracks, stats);

A clip without a base needs only its transform space: the compress_track_list overload without a base uses it.

Pre-processing and the error measurement (calculate_compression_error) also use the transform space of the track array. Give them the same base as compression (pre_process_settings_t::transform_base).

With a built-in format, compression and the error measurement combine each transform with its base with apply_additive_to_base (see here). They do not normalize the result. Thus the measured error is the error of your runtime when it uses the same function and does not normalize the result.

docs.title: Relative additive clips
docs.text:
Clips in this space are applied on top of their base clip with a simple multiplication:

result = additive * base

This is the standard way to represent things in local space of something else. For example, every bone is in relative and local space of its parent bone. To convert a bone from local space to its parent space, we multiply them.

docs.title: Additive 0
docs.text:
I couldn't come up with a better name for this, suggestions welcome!

Clips in this space have their rotations multiplied with the base, the translations are added, and the scale is combined as follow:

scale = additive_scale * base_scale

Among others, this mode is used by ozz-animation.

docs.title: Additive 1
docs.text:
I couldn't come up with a better name for this, suggestions welcome!

Clips in this space have their rotations multiplied with the base, the translations are added, and the scale is combined as follow:

scale = (1.0 + additive_scale) * base_scale

This is the additive mode used by Unreal 4.

docs.title: Custom base format
docs.text:
When your runtime combines a clip with its base in another way, implement an itransform_base_adapter_t (see here). Set the base format to custom, and set adapter in the base description:

class my_base_adapter final : public itransform_base_adapter_t
{
public:
    virtual const char* get_name() const override { return "my_base_adapter"; }

    // The scale of a sample without scale, 0.0 or 1.0 (defaults to 1.0)
    virtual float get_default_scale() const override { return 1.0F; }

    virtual rtm::vqvf apply_base(uint32_t transform_index, const rtm::vqvf& base_transform, const rtm::vqvf& transform) const override
    {
        // The root does not use the base
        if (transform_index == 0)
            return transform;

        return transform_add0(base_transform, transform);
    }
};

my_base_adapter base_adapter;

transform_base_desc_t transform_base;
transform_base.format = additive_clip_format8::custom;
transform_base.tracks = &base_track_list;
transform_base.adapter = &base_adapter;

The adapter combines one transform at a time:

  • Compression puts the base in the transform space of the clip first, as with the other formats. The base transform and the clip transform that the adapter receives are in the same space. Then compression puts the combined transforms in object space. Thus the adapter does not need the transform hierarchy.
  • The transform index lets the adapter combine some transforms in another way, for example the root.
  • The default scale is the scale of the samples of a track without scale (for example, a vqf track). Decompression returns it when the compressed tracks have no scale. The compressed data keeps one bit for it, thus it must be 0.0 or 1.0.
  • When the clip and the base have no scale, compression ignores the scale of the combined transform.
  • Compression calls the adapter in its inner loops, with the raw and the lossy samples. The same input must always give the same output.
  • Compression and the error measurement use the combined transform as is: they do not normalize its rotation. Thus the measured error is the error of your runtime when it combines the transforms with the same function. If your runtime normalizes the combined transform, the adapter must normalize it too.

The custom base format has these limits:

  • The legacy error metric (compression_settings::error_metric) does not support it. Compression and pre-processing return an error.
  • The deprecated compress_track_list overload that takes an additive base and an additive format cannot receive an adapter. It returns an error with the custom format.
  • A clip file can hold the custom format name, but not the adapter. Your tool must supply the adapter.

docs.title: Algorithm: uniformly sampled
docs.text:
The uniformly sampled algorithm is by far the simplest. A clip is sampled at a fixed internal (e.g. 30 FPS) and each sample is retained. Constant tracks are compacted to a single sample and default tracks are dropped.

Compression is achieved by storing the samples on a reduced number of bits using the various rotation and vector formats.

Decompression is very fast because the data is uniformly spaced. Each sample is sorted by time and by track to ensure that when we sample a specific point in time, all the relevant samples are contiguous in memory for optimal cache locality during decompression. This also means that the decompression performance is independent of the playback direction. It will be the same when playing forward, backward, and randomly.

docs.title: Data and method used
docs.text:
To compile the statistics, the animation database from Carnegie-Mellon University is used. The raw animation clips in FBX form can be found on the Unity asset store here. They were converted to the ACL file format using the fbx2acl script. Data available upon request, it is far too large for GitHub.

  • Number of clips: 2534
  • Sample rate: 24 FPS
  • Total duration: 9h 49m 37.58s
  • Raw size: 1429.38 MB (10x float32 * num bones * num samples)

ACL supports various compression methods but only the overall best variant will be tracked here (see get_default_compression_settings() for details).

The error is measured 3cm away from each bone to simulate the visual mesh skinning process as described here with the default error threshold of 0.01cm. The 99th percentile and the number of samples below the error threshold are calculated by measuring the error on every bone at every sample.

The performance of ACL in Unreal Engine is tracked by the plugin here.

docs.title: Compressing raw tracks
docs.text:
Once you have created a raw track list and an allocator instance, you are ready to compress it.

For now, we only implement a single algorithm: uniformly sampled. This is a simple and excellent algorithm to use for everyday animation clips.

Note that before compression, it is recommended to pre-process your raw tracks.

docs.title: Compressing raw scalar tracks
docs.text:
Scalar tracks use only some of the compression settings: scalar_format, optimize_loops, and metadata. With the scalarf_variable format (see get_default_compression_settings()), each animated track uses the lowest bit rate that keeps its precision. With the scalarf_full format, each animated track keeps its samples with full precision. Like the transform formats, compression_settings defaults to full precision.

Scalar tracks can also use extended samples to select how each sample interpolates.

Segmenting is currently not supported by scalar tracks.

#include <acl/compression/compress.h>

using namespace acl;

compression_settings settings = get_default_compression_settings();

OutputStats stats;
compressed_tracks* out_compressed_tracks = nullptr;
ErrorResult result = compress_track_list(allocator, raw_track_list, settings, out_compressed_tracks, stats);

docs.title: Compressing raw transform tracks
docs.text:
The compression level used will dictate how much time to spend optimizing the variable bit rates. Lower levels are faster but produce a larger compressed size.

While we support various rotation and vector quantization formats, the variable variants are generally the best. It is safe to use them for all your clips but if you do happen to run into issues with some exotic clips, you can easily fallback to less aggressive variants.

Selecting the right runtime transform type is important: select the one that your game engine uses to compose transforms. With transform_runtime_type_t::automatic (the default), compression uses exact VQM arithmetic when scale is present (or VQS arithmetic with vqsf raw tracks). Without scale, it uses VQ arithmetic and measures the exact error. Select another type only when your game engine composes transforms differently (for example, transform_runtime_type_t::vqvf for VQV arithmetic that discards the shear).

The last important setting to choose is the error_threshold. This is used in conjunction with the transform metric and the virtual vertex distance (shell distance) in order to guarantee that a certain quality is maintained. A default value of 0.01cm is safe to use and it most likely should never be changed unless the units you are using differ. If you do run into issues where compression artifacts are visible, in all likelihood the virtual vertex distance used on the problematic bones is not conservative enough.

#include <acl/compression/compress.h>

using namespace acl;

compression_settings settings;
settings.level = compression_level8::medium;
settings.rotation_format = rotation_format8::quatf_drop_w_variable;
settings.translation_format = vector_format8::vector3f_variable;
settings.scale_format = vector_format8::vector3f_variable;

// Optional: the default 'automatic' uses VQM arithmetic with scale
// settings.transform_runtime_type = transform_runtime_type_t::vqvf;

output_stats stats;
compressed_tracks* out_compressed_tracks = nullptr;
error_result result = compress_track_list(allocator, raw_track_list, settings, out_compressed_tracks, stats);

You can also query the current default and recommended settings with this function: get_default_compression_settings().

docs.title: Peak memory usage
docs.text:
Compression allocates temporary buffers. The largest clips use many times their raw size. When many clips compress in parallel, the sum of these buffers can cause the system to write memory pages to disk.

Use estimate_compression_peak_memory_usage(..) to find the memory that a clip needs before you compress it. It takes the same tracks, settings, and base as compress_track_list(..). It does not allocate memory, and its cost is low compared to compression. For example, a scheduler can start a new compression only when the sum of the estimates is less than a memory budget.

#include <acl/compression/compress.h>

using namespace acl;

const size_t peak_memory_usage = estimate_compression_peak_memory_usage(raw_track_list, settings);

The overload with a track list reads the sizes, the hierarchy, and the names of the tracks, not their samples. To decide before you load the tracks, use the overload with a compression_memory_desc_t. Fill it from the metadata of the asset: the track type, the number of tracks, and the number of samples are required. The other values are optional. Except for total_name_length, each default value gives the largest estimate:

  • max_hierarchy_depth: the largest number of ancestors of a transform. Without it, the estimate uses a single chain of transforms, and some buffers grow with the square of the number of transforms.
  • total_name_length: the length of the names. Set it when the metadata settings include the names.
  • looping_policy, transform_space, and the values of the base (base_format, num_base_tracks, num_base_samples_per_track, base_has_non_uniform_scale).
#include <acl/compression/compress.h>

using namespace acl;

compression_memory_desc_t desc;
desc.track_type = track_type8::vqvf;
desc.num_tracks = num_bones;
desc.num_samples_per_track = num_frames;
desc.max_hierarchy_depth = max_bone_depth;  // Optional

const size_t peak_memory_usage = estimate_compression_peak_memory_usage(desc, settings);

On a large set of production clips, the estimate with only the track type and the numbers of tracks and samples is 2% larger than the estimate with the track list for the median clip, and at most 17% larger. With max_hierarchy_depth too, the two estimates are equal.

The value is the largest sum of the live allocations that compression requests from its allocator. It does not include the overhead of the allocator, the raw tracks, or the statistics of output_stats::logging. The estimate cannot know which tracks are constant before compression, thus it assumes that each track is animated. The value is usually larger than the real peak. On a large set of production clips with the default settings, the estimate is 9% to 118% larger than the measured peak, and 58% larger for the median clip.

docs.title: Configuration macros
docs.text:
ACL is a header-only library, thus macros configure it. Define a macro on the command line of the compiler (for example -DACL_USE_POPCOUNT), or before you include the first ACL header. acl/config.h lists the macros with more details.

All the C++ files of a program must use the same macros. Otherwise, the same function can have different definitions in two files, and the behavior is undefined.

ACL uses Realtime Math (RTM) for its math. The RTM macros (for example RTM_NO_INTRINSICS or RTM_ON_ASSERT_THROW) also apply to the code of ACL.

docs.title: Asserts
docs.text:
By default, ACL removes its asserts at compile time. Define one of these macros to keep them. An assert is fatal: if the program continues after an assert fails, the behavior is undefined. See handling asserts.

Macro Effect ACL_ON_ASSERT_ABORT A failed assert prints its message to stderr and calls std::abort(). ACL_ON_ASSERT_THROW A failed assert throws an acl::runtime_assert exception. ACL_ON_ASSERT_CUSTOM A failed assert calls the function that the macro names. Its signature is void on_assert(const char* expression, int line, const char* file, const char* format, ...). ACL_ASSERT With ACL_ON_ASSERT_CUSTOM, define ACL_ASSERT(expression, format, ...) to replace the complete assert implementation. ACL_ASSERT_STRING_FORMAT_SPECIFIER The format specifier that the assert messages use for a const char* argument. The default is "%s". With a custom function that expects wide strings, MSVC can use "%hs".

When one of the first three macros is defined, ACL defines ACL_HAS_ASSERT_CHECKS. Your code can test it.

docs.title: Hardware features
docs.text:
ACL detects the SIMD instruction sets with RTM. These macros enable x86 and x64 instructions that RTM does not detect.

Macro Effect ACL_USE_POPCOUNT Use the popcnt and lzcnt instructions to count bits. If the processor does not support them, the behavior is undefined. Windows 11 requires them. ACL defines this macro on Xbox One. ACL_BMI_INTRINSICS Use the BMI instructions. If the processor does not support them, the behavior is undefined. Windows 11 requires them. ACL defines this macro on Xbox One, when the compiler defines __BMI__ (for example with -mbmi), and with MSVC when AVX is enabled. ACL_NO_8_WIDE_AVX Do not use the 8-wide AVX instructions when AVX is enabled. On older processors that split each 8-wide instruction in two (for example AMD Jaguar), the 4-wide code can be faster.

Both ACL_USE_POPCOUNT and ACL_BMI_INTRINSICS stop the compilation on a processor that is not x86 or x64.

docs.title: Decompression performance
docs.text: Macro Effect ACL_NO_EARLY_PREFETCHING Do not start the memory prefetches as early as possible during decompression. ACL starts them early on all platforms except x86 and x64. On a processor with a high clock rate, the code can be faster without early prefetches.

docs.title: Clip files
docs.text: Macro Effect ACL_USE_SJSON Compile the clip reader and the clip writer in acl/io/. They read and write the ACL file format. The sjson-cpp headers must be on the include path. Without this macro, the headers in acl/io/ are empty.

docs.title: Namespace and versions
docs.text: Macro Effect ACL_ENABLE_VERSION_NAMESPACE Put the code of ACL in a versioned namespace in acl (for example acl::v2199). By default, the namespace is inline: client code still uses acl::. Two versions of ACL can then be in the same program. ACL_NO_INLINE_NAMESPACE With ACL_ENABLE_VERSION_NAMESPACE, the versioned namespace is not inline: client code must use the versioned name. ACL_NO_VERSION_NAMESPACE Do not use a versioned namespace, even when ACL_ENABLE_VERSION_NAMESPACE is defined. ACL defines this macro with Visual Studio 2015. ACL_NO_DEPRECATION Do not show deprecation warnings when your code uses deprecated API. ACL_USE_CPP11_STD_MEMORY_ORDER With C++20 or later, use the C++11 names of std::memory_order. Use it when a modern compiler uses an older standard library that does not have the C++20 names.

docs.title: Allocator debugging
docs.text:
These macros control the checks of acl::ansi_allocator. The sanitizing and the tracking are active only when an assert macro is defined.

Macro Effect ACL_NO_ALLOCATOR_SANITIZING Do not fill new memory with 0xCD and freed memory with 0xFE. These patterns help to find uninitialized memory and the use of freed memory. ACL_NO_ALLOCATOR_TRACKING Do not count the allocations and the deallocations. The count helps to find memory leaks and memory that is freed twice. ACL_ALLOCATOR_TRACK_ALL_ALLOCATIONS Record each allocation, to find memory leaks and memory that is freed twice. Use it only to debug: it is slow.

docs.title: Creating a raw track list
docs.text:
Once you have an allocator instance, the next step is to create a raw track list and populate it with the data we will want to compress. Doing so is fairly straight forward and you will only need a few things:

  • An allocator instance
  • The number of tracks (a track array cannot be resized)
  • The number of samples per track (each track has the same number of samples)
  • The rate at which samples are recorded (e.g. 30 == 30 FPS)
  • Access to the Realtime Math headers since its types are used by the API
#include <acl/compression/track_array.h>

using namespace acl;

uint32_t num_tracks = 4;
uint32_t num_samples_per_track = 20;
float sample_rate = 30.0f;
track_array_float3f raw_track_list(allocator, num_tracks);

Once you have created an instance, simply populate the track data. Note that at the moment, tracks contained in the array are untyped but they must all have the same track type (e.g. float2f), the same number of samples per track, and the same sample rate.

Each track requires a track description. It contains a number of important properties:

  • output_index: after compression, this is the index of the track. This allows re-ordering for LOD processing and other similar use cases.
  • parent_index: for transform tracks, indicates the parent transform index it is relative to (in local space of).
  • precision: the precision we aim to attain when optimizing the bit rate. The resulting compression error is nearly guaranteed to be below this threshold.
  • shell_distance: for transform tracks, indicates the distance at which we measure the error, see error metric function.
track_desc_scalarf desc0;
desc0.output_index = 0;
desc0.precision = 0.001F;

track_desc_transformf desc1;
desc1.output_index = 0;
desc1.parent_index = 0;
desc1.precision = 0.01F;
desc1.shell_distance = 3.0F;

Tracks can be created in one of four ways:

  • make_copy(..): creates a new track and copies the data internally. The new instance owns the memory and the original data is no longer required.
  • make_reserve(..): creates a new track and allocates the required memory without initializing it. It owns the new allocated memory.
  • make_owner(..): creates a new track and takes ownership of the provided source pointer. No copy takes place.
  • make_ref(..): creates a new track and references the provided source data. No copy takes place and the new instance does not own the referenced memory.

make_owner(..) and make_ref(..) are handy when the track data is already allocated somewhere and doesn't need to be copied explicitly. Functions that take source data as input also support a custom stride and make no assumption about the data layout for utmost flexibility.

track_float3f raw_track0 = track_float3f::make_reserve(desc0, allocator, num_samples, sample_rate);
raw_track0[0] = rtm::float3f{ 1.0F, 3123.0F, 315.13F };
raw_track0[1] = rtm::float3f{ 2.333F, 321.13F, 31.66F };
raw_track0[2] = rtm::float3f{ 3.123F, 81.0F, 913.13F };
raw_track0[3] = rtm::float3f{ 4.5F, 91.13F, 41.135F };
// ...
raw_track_list[0] = std::move(raw_track0);

Once your raw track list has been populated with data, it is ready for compression. The data contained within the track_array will be read-only.

Each sample of a scalar track can also select how it interpolates to the next sample, for example to make a step. See extended samples for details.

You can override the looping policy by calling raw_track_list.set_looping_policy(policy);. This is only necessary if you perform your own loop optimization before compressing with ACL. See how to handle looping playback for details.

docs.title: Transform tracks
docs.text:
ACL supports three transform track types:

  • vqvf (track_vqvf, track_array_vqvf): each sample is a rtm::vqvf with a rotation, a translation, and a 3D scale.
  • vqsf (track_vqsf, track_array_vqsf): each sample is a rtm::vqsf with a rotation, a translation, and a uniform scale. The scale is in the W component of translation_scale.
  • vqf (track_vqf, track_array_vqf): each sample is a rtm::vqf with a rotation and a translation. A VQ track has no scale.

The three types use track_desc_transformf as their description. With vqf, ACL ignores the scale of default_value. With vqsf, ACL uses the X component of the scale of default_value.

The compressed tracks keep the type of the raw tracks. Thus a VQV clip without scale gives a compressed VQV clip. To convert the raw tracks from one type to another, use the convert_transform_type pre-process action.

When you decompress a VQ clip, ACL does not write the scale: it does not call write_scale on your track writer. If you use your own decompression settings, is_track_type_supported must return true for track_type8::vqf to decompress a VQ clip.

A compressed VQS clip stores one value for each scale sample, thus an animated uniform scale uses a third of the memory of a VQV scale. When you decompress a VQS clip, ACL writes the scale with this overload of your track writer:

void RTM_SIMD_CALL write_scale(uint32_t track_index, rtm::scalarf_arg0 scale);

When your track writer does not have this overload, ACL calls write_scale(uint32_t, rtm::vector4f_arg0) with the uniform scale in [xyzw]. If you use your own decompression settings, is_track_type_supported must return true for track_type8::vqsf to decompress a VQS clip. The default decompression settings for transform tracks accept the three types.

track_desc_transformf desc;
desc.output_index = 0;
desc.precision = 0.01F;
desc.shell_distance = 3.0F;

track_array_vqf raw_transform_tracks(allocator, num_tracks);

track_vqf raw_track = track_vqf::make_reserve(desc, allocator, num_samples, sample_rate);
raw_track[0] = rtm::vq_set(rtm::quat_identity(), rtm::vector_set(0.0F, 1.0F, 0.0F));
// ...
raw_transform_tracks[0] = std::move(raw_track);

docs.title: Playback scale
docs.text:
The runtime can play a clip at another scale than the scale of its authoring. For example, a designer scales a boss character, or the game spawns a character with a random scale. Then the error that you see is the object space error multiplied by that scale. Set the uniform scale of the clip at playback with set_playback_scale(..) on the track array:

track_array_vqvf raw_transform_tracks(allocator, num_tracks);
// ...
raw_transform_tracks.set_playback_scale(4.0F);
  • The precision of each track, the keyframe stripping threshold, and the error that calculate_compression_error returns are in playback units. Thus a precision of 0.01 keeps the error at playback below 0.01.
  • The shell distance stays in the units of the clip.
  • Compression divides the precision by the playback scale: with a scale of 4.0 and a precision of 0.01, it compresses the clip as with a precision of 0.0025 and a scale of 1.0.
  • The compressed data does not store the playback scale: decompression does not use it. The track descriptions in the compressed data keep the precision that you set.
  • The playback scale must be positive and finite. It defaults to 1.0. Scalar tracks do not use it.
  • To compare two raw track arrays with calculate_compression_error, both must have the same playback scale.

When the clip plays at different scales, use the largest scale.

docs.title: Additive animation clips
docs.text:
If the clip you are compressing is an additive clip, you will also need to create an instance for the base clip. Put the base clip and the format of the additive clip in a transform_base_desc_t, and give it to compress_track_list(..). See the transform space for an example.

When the transforms of the clip are not in local space, set the transform space of the track array with set_transform_space(..). See the transform space.

The library assumes that the raw clip data has already been transformed to be in additive or relative space.

The additive clip and its base clip can have different transform types (vqvf, vqsf, or vqf). A VQ track has no scale: in an additive clip, ACL uses the identity scale of the additive format (0.0 with additive1, 1.0 otherwise). In the base clip, ACL uses a scale of 1.0.

Note that if your additive format does not use a scale of 1.0 as its default value, you will need to provide the desired value to ACL. See default sub-track handling for details.

docs.title: Re-ordering or stripping bones
docs.text:
Sometimes it is desirable to re-order the bones being outputted or strip them altogether. This could be to facilitate LOD support or various forms of skeleton changes without needing to re-import the clips. This is easily achieved by setting the desired output_index on each track_desc_transformf contained in a track_vqvf, a track_vqsf, or a track_vqf. The default value is the track index. You can use k_invalid_track_index to strip the track from the final compressed output.

Note that each output_index needs to be unique and there can be no gaps. If 20 bones are outputted, the indices must run from [0 .. 20).

docs.title: Compressing morph target blend weights
docs.text:
Curves that drive a morph target (aka blend shape) are not ordinary and require special consideration. They ultimately drive an object space mesh deformation and as such we can leverage that information to reduce the memory footprint and simplify the task of choosing a suitable precision value.

If you have access to the morph target deformation information, you can calculate the largest vertex displacement for a given curve. Once you have that value, use a morph target deformation precision value such as 0.1 mm and use the maximum vertex displacement to calculate the desired blend weight precision value like this:

blend weight precision = vertex precision / vertex displacement delta

See here for more details.

docs.title: Using custom default sub-track values
docs.text: By default, ACL assumes that sub-tracks have the identity as their default value. This is nice and simple but it is not always optimal. If a character has many animation compressed, it might be better to use its bind pose as the default value instead. See default sub-track handling for details.

docs.title: Database and streaming support
docs.text:
ACL 2.0 now supports compressing multiple animation clips into a single database to facilitate streaming as well as data stripping. See here for details on what it can do and how it works.

See here to take a look at how the UE4 plugin supports it.

docs.title: How to build a database
docs.text:
In order to be able to build a database with the right key frames, metadata must be added during compression. To do so, make sure to enable include_contributing_error inside your acl::compression_settings.

acl::compression_settings settings = acl::get_default_compression_settings();
settings.include_contributing_error = true;

This will add metadata to the compressed byte stream which will later be stripped once the database is created. Its footprint is only temporary as it isn't needed at runtime when decompressing.

The database creation API is exposed in acl/compression/compress.h.

First, use build_database(..) to create a database. It takes as input the compressed animation clips you wish to merge and it will output new compressed animation clips and the database they are bound to. All of these buffers are binary blobs and can be moved around with std::memcpy safely. The only requirement is that they be 16 bytes aligned.

Once the database is created, its bulk data (the part that can be optionally streamed) will be part of the database byte buffer. To strip it into a separate buffer that can be omitted or streamed later, use split_database_bulk_data(..). This will output a new database along with its two bulk data buffers.

If some quality tiers aren't necessary on your platform of choice (e.g. mobile), you can strip them by calling strip_database_quality_tier(..). The bulk data does not change and if it had been stripped, the stripped tier's buffer can simply be freed.

docs.title: Decompressing with a database
docs.text:
At runtime, animation clips that are bound to a database can be decompressed without the database. If you attempt to do so, only the data within the clip will be used (lowest visual quality).

In order to use a database, a acl::database_context must be created for it.

const acl::compressed_database* database = ...
acl::iallocator& allocator = ...

acl::database_context<acl::default_database_settings> database_context;
database_context.initialize(allocator, *database);

The above will work if the database contains its bulk data inline (if it hasn't been stripped). To support streaming (whether from memory, memory mapped, network, or other IO) a acl::database_streamer must be provided. See the linked header for details on how to implement it.

acl::null_database_streamer medium_streamer(medium_data, medium_data_size);
acl::null_database_streamer low_streamer(low_data, low_data_size);

acl::database_context<acl::default_database_settings> database_context;
database_context.initialize(allocator, *database, medium_streamer, low_streamer);

If a quality tier has been stripped, its streamer will never be used and any streamer can be provided. Streamers must live as long as the database does. The streamers are responsible for streaming data in and out.

When the time comes to decompress, simply provide the database context alongside the compressed tracks data and make sure database support is enabled in your decompression settings (by default that code is stripped).

struct my_decompression_settings : acl::default_transform_decompression_settings
{
    using database_settings_type = default_database_settings;
};

const acl::compressed_tracks* compressed_clip_data = ...

acl::decompression_context<my_decompression_settings> context;
context.initialize(compressed_clip_data, database_context);

The rest of the decompression code remains unchanged.

It is safe to stream in data while decompression is in progress. Doing so it thread safe. However, only a single stream in/out request can be in flight at a time and streaming out cannot be done while decompression is in progress.

Once a streamer finishes a read request (e.g. file IO), it can complete the stream request from any thread.

docs.title: Decompressing a track list
docs.text:
Once you have a compressed track list, the first order of business to decompress it is to select a set of decompression_settings. The decompression settings struct is populated with constexpr functions that can be overridden to turn on or off the code generation per feature.

The next thing you need is a decompression_context instance. This will allow you to actually decompress tracks. You can also use it to seek arbitrarily in the list. For safety, the decompression context is templated with the decompression settings.

#include "acl/decompression/decompress.h"

using namespace acl;

decompression_context<default_decompression_settings> context;

context.initialize(*tracks);
context.seek(sample_time, sample_rounding_policy::none);

// create an instance of 'track_writer' so we can write the output somewhere
context.decompress_track(track_index, my_track_writer); // a single track
context.decompress_tracks(my_track_writer); // all tracks

As shown, a context must be initialized with a compressed track list instance. Some context objects such as the one used by uniform sampling can be re-used by any compressed track list and does not need to be re-created while others might require this. In order to detect when this might be required, the function is_bound_to(const compressed_tracks& tracks) is provided. Some context objects cannot be created on the stack and must be dynamically allocated with an allocator instance. The functions make_decompression_context(...) are provided for this purpose.

You can seek anywhere in a track list but you will need to handle looping manually in your game engine (e.g. by calling fmod). When seeking, you must also provide a sample_rounding_policy to dictate how the interpolation is to be performed. See here for details. ACL handles various rounding modes: none will interpolate, floor will return the first sample before the sample time (when you need to step animations frame by frame), ceil will return the first sample after the sample time, nearest will return the closest sample to the sample time, and per_track allows you to specify through the track_writer the rounding mode per track. See also handling per track rounding. With extended samples, a constant sample changes the output of the none policy.

You can override the looping policy by calling context.set_looping_policy(policy);. This is only necessary if you perform your own loop optimization before compressing with ACL. See how to handle looping playback for details.

Every decompression function supported by the context is prefixed with decompress_*. A track_writer is used for optimized output writing. You can implement your own and coerce to your own math types. The type is templated on the decompress_* functions in order to be easily inlined.

The API is the same for scalar and joint transform tracks. For optimal code generation, ensure the decompression settings used are tuned to the expected data. See the header where it is defined for more information.

docs.title: Floating point exceptions
docs.text: For performance reasons, the decompression code assumes that the caller has already disabled all floating point exceptions. This avoids the need to save/restore them with every call. ACL provides helpers in acl/core/floating_point_control.h to assist and optionally this behavior can be controlled by overriding decompression_settings::disable_fp_exeptions().

docs.title: Backwards compatibility
docs.text:
By default, decompression will support every ACL version prior to and including ACL 2.0. If you wish to only support a single version and to strip the unnecessary code, you can specify your own decompression settings struct along with the desired static constexpr compressed_tracks_version16 version_supported() { return compressed_tracks_version16::any; } implementation.

There is no backwards compatibility support for ACL 1.3 and earlier.

docs.title: Default sub-track handling
docs.text:
When a joint track is compressed, it is split into 3 sub-tracks: rotation, translation, scale. Each of these can be in one of three categories: animated (N samples retained), constant (1 sample retained), or default (0 sample retained). Because default sub-tracks do not store a sample, they are the most compact and leveraging them to their full extent allows for significant memory savings.

The default values are the identity but that is not always optimal. A better choice is whatever default value your integrating code base uses. A common choice is the character bind pose (e.g. T-stance).

Note that some additive formats do not use a scale of 1.0 as their default value and for those clips, overriding the default value will be required for proper usage.

docs.title: Tuning the compression
docs.text: Telling ACL what default values you use is simple. When you create the raw tracks array, simply specify it in the track_desc_transformf by setting the default_value member. ACL will use that value during compression but it will NOT be included in the compressed data stream since we do not store default samples. You will need to provide it again during decompression.

docs.title: Handling decompression
docs.text:
If you use a default value that differs from the identity, you will need to provide it to ACL during decompression. This can be done in a number of ways through the track_writer implementation you provide when sampling tracks.

These are the members you must override and implement:

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// If default sub-tracks aren't skipped, a value must be written. Either
// they are constant for every sub-track (e.g. identity) or they vary per
// sub-track (e.g. bind pose).
// By default, default sub-tracks are constant and the identity.
// Must be static constexpr!
static constexpr default_sub_track_mode get_default_rotation_mode() { return default_sub_track_mode::constant; }
static constexpr default_sub_track_mode get_default_translation_mode() { return default_sub_track_mode::constant; }
static constexpr default_sub_track_mode get_default_scale_mode() { return default_sub_track_mode::legacy; }

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// If default sub-tracks are constant, these functions return their value.
rtm::quatf RTM_SIMD_CALL get_constant_default_rotation() const { return rtm::quat_identity(); }
rtm::vector4f RTM_SIMD_CALL get_constant_default_translation() const { return rtm::vector_zero(); }
rtm::vector4f RTM_SIMD_CALL get_constant_default_scale() const { return rtm::vector_set(1.0F); }

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// If default sub-tracks are variable, these functions return their value.
rtm::quatf RTM_SIMD_CALL get_variable_default_rotation(uint32_t /*track_index*/) const { return rtm::quat_identity(); }
rtm::vector4f RTM_SIMD_CALL get_variable_default_translation(uint32_t /*track_index*/) const { return rtm::vector_zero(); }
rtm::vector4f RTM_SIMD_CALL get_variable_default_scale(uint32_t /*track_index*/) const { return rtm::vector_set(1.0F); }

The sub-track mode dictates how default sub-tracks are handled. A sub-track can be skipped and ACL won't attempt to write it (suitable when the default values are already in the output buffer), they can be constant and identical for all sub-tracks of that type (the default behavior, suitable for ordinary clips and additive clips), and variable where each sub-track can have its own default value. A value of legacy can be used for scale for the time being but this is meant for backwards compatibility only and will be removed in the future.

If sub-tracks aren't skipped, ACL will query what the default value is (whether constant or variable) and it will write it out to the output buffer as it would normally. Skipping sub-tracks is handy if the output buffer is pre-populated with the default values. This may or may not be faster depending on your integration and whether or not ACL needs to perform an indirection lookup with the track index.

docs.title: Transform error metric
docs.text:
A good error metric is necessary for each animation compression algorithm, and ACL is no different. ACL uses the technique that this blog post describes. ACL measures the error on a rigid shell around each transform: a sphere at a certain distance from the transform (the shell_distance of the track).

To measure the error of a clip, compression must know two things:

  • How your runtime composes the local space transforms into object space: the runtime transform type. A transform adapter gives the operations of this type.
  • How to measure the error between a raw and a lossy transform: the transform metric. See transform_metrics.h.

Select the runtime transform type that your runtime uses. When the error that ACL measures is not the error of your runtime, the visual quality can be lower.

docs.title: Runtime transform types
docs.text:
compression_settings::transform_runtime_type selects the runtime transform type (transform_runtime_type_t):

  • vqf: a rotation and a translation, stored as rtm::vqvf. The scale is not used.
  • vqsf: a rotation, a translation, and a uniform scale, stored as rtm::vqsf. You can select it only with vqsf raw tracks.
  • vqvf: a rotation, a translation, and a 3D scale, stored as rtm::vqvf. The product of two transforms discards the shear, as in many game engines.
  • vqmf: a rotation, a translation, and a 3x3 scale/shear matrix, stored as rtm::vqmf. The product keeps the shear. Thus the object space transforms are exact.
  • matrix3x4f: a 3x4 affine matrix, stored as rtm::matrix3x4f. The product keeps the shear.
  • custom: your own type. Compression uses compression_settings::custom_transform_adapter.
  • automatic (the default): compression selects the type from the raw tracks. It selects vqsf for vqsf raw tracks when the additive base (if any) has a uniform scale. Otherwise, it selects vqmf.

When a clip has no scale, each built-in runtime transform type gives the same transforms. Thus compression uses vqf, the fastest type, when the transform metric supports it. Compression makes this selection for each segment: a segment without scale uses vqf, also when other segments of the clip have scale.

Compression always uses a custom transform adapter, also in a segment without scale. Your transforms can use data that the source scale does not show. For example, your adapter can add a value that you compress in another track.

Compression always converts rtm::vqvf source transforms into the runtime transform type. With VQ raw tracks (vqf), the source scale is 1.0, or 0.0 in an additive1 clip. With VQS raw tracks (vqsf), the source scale holds the uniform scale in [xyz].

docs.title: Transform metrics
docs.text:
compression_settings::transform_metric selects the transform metric. When it is nullptr (the default), compression uses the default metric of the runtime transform type:

  • precise_transform_metric with vqf and vqsf. It finds the point on the sphere with the largest error and it computes with float64. With vqf, the result is exact. With vqsf, when the raw and lossy scales are not equal, the result can be above the exact error. The difference is not more than |s1 - s0| * shell_distance.
  • shell_transform_metric with vqvf, vqmf, matrix3x4f, and custom. It transforms points on the sphere with the raw and lossy transforms and returns the largest distance. Without scale (vqf), it uses two points. Otherwise, it uses three points: one on each axis. The result is an approximation of the error.

shell_transform_metric supports each runtime transform type. precise_transform_metric supports only vqf and vqsf. Compression returns an error when the metric does not support the runtime transform type.

docs.title: Additive clips
docs.text:
ACL applies the additive to the base on the rtm::vqvf source transforms. Then it converts the result into the runtime transform type. See here for the additive formats and how to select the one for your game engine.

For the purpose of measuring the error, we ignore object space additive blending. It typically does not play a significant role in the resulting error because the pose is fundamentally very close. As such, the additive clip is always applied in local space to the base clip.

docs.title: Measuring the error of compressed tracks
docs.text:
To measure the error as compression does, give your compression settings to calculate_compression_error. The function uses the transform space of the raw tracks. An additive clip also needs the base description that you gave to compression, with its base and its additive format (see here):

const track_error error = calculate_compression_error(allocator, raw_tracks, context, settings);
const track_error additive_error = calculate_compression_error(allocator, raw_tracks, context, settings, transform_base);

Pre-processing uses the same settings: pre_process_settings_t::transform_runtime_type, custom_transform_adapter, and transform_metric. Use the same values for pre-processing and compression.

docs.title: Implementing your own runtime transform type
docs.text:
Find how your game engine combines the local space transforms into object space. Then implement a class that derives from itransform_adapter. The built-in transform adapters in transform_adapters.h are examples. Then select transform_runtime_type_t::custom and set compression_settings::custom_transform_adapter.

The adapter gives these operations:

  • get_transform_size: the size of your transform type. Its alignment must be 16 bytes or less.
  • convert_transforms: converts rtm::vqvf source transforms into your type. When your type is rtm::vqvf, return false from needs_conversion. Compression then does not call convert_transforms.
  • identity and mul: the identity transform and the product of two transforms. The output of mul can be one of its inputs.
  • local_to_object_space: optional, the default implementation uses mul.
  • mul_point3_x4: transforms four points. shell_transform_metric uses it.
  • is_associative: whether or not the product of your type is associative.

When the product is associative, compression keeps the object space transforms in a cache, and it updates only what changes. When the product is not associative, compression must multiply the full transform chain for each bit rate that it tests. This is slower.

With a custom transform adapter, compression calls the adapter through its virtual functions. With a built-in transform adapter and a built-in transform metric, compression uses code without virtual function calls. This code is faster.

docs.title: Implementing your own transform metric
docs.text:
Implement a class that derives from itransform_metric, and set compression_settings::transform_metric. The built-in transform metrics in transform_metrics.h are examples.

  • is_supported: returns whether or not the metric can measure transforms of a transform adapter.
  • calculate_error_squared: returns the squared error between the raw and the lossy transform. Use the transform adapter in the arguments to read the transforms.

Compression calls your transform metric through its virtual functions. This is also true for an instance of a built-in metric that you set in the settings. To use the faster code of a built-in metric, keep transform_metric at nullptr and use the default metric.

docs.title: Legacy error metrics (deprecated)
docs.text:
A legacy error metric (itransform_error_metric) combines the runtime transform type and the error measurement in one interface. These parts of the API are deprecated, and ACL 2.3 will remove them:

  • compression_settings::error_metric and pre_process_settings_t::error_metric
  • itransform_error_metric and the legacy error metrics: vqvf_transform_error_metric, vqvf_precise_transform_error_metric, vqvf_matrix3x4f_transform_error_metric, and additive_vqvf_transform_error_metric
  • The calculate_compression_error overloads that take an itransform_error_metric: use the overloads that take the compression settings

When you set a legacy error metric in the settings, you cannot set transform_runtime_type, custom_transform_adapter, or transform_metric.

To migrate, select the runtime transform type of your legacy error metric:

Legacy error metric Runtime transform type Transform metric vqvf_transform_error_metric and its additive variant vqvf nullptr (shell) vqvf_matrix3x4f_transform_error_metric matrix3x4f nullptr (shell) vqvf_precise_transform_error_metric vqf or automatic (without scale) nullptr (precise) Your own error metric custom with your transform adapter your transform metric, or nullptr (shell)

With the runtime transform type, compression applies the additive base itself. You do not need a variant for each additive format.

The bit rate algorithm v2 supports the legacy error metrics that return true from supports_bit_rate_algorithm_v2. The other legacy error metrics use the slower bit rate algorithm v1. Of the built-in legacy error metrics, only vqvf_matrix3x4f_transform_error_metric returns false. Your own error metric also returns false, unless it overrides the function. With the runtime transform type, compression always uses the bit rate algorithm v2.

docs.title: Extended samples
docs.text:
ACL keeps the samples of a track at uniform intervals and does not store a time for each sample. By default, each sample interpolates linearly to the next sample. An extended track adds an interpolator to each sample. The interpolator of a sample controls the interval from that sample to the next sample.

Only scalar tracks support extended samples (float1f, float2f, float3f, float4f, and vector4f). Transform tracks (vqvf) do not support them, and track_vqvf_ex does not compile.

See also issue #526 for the design notes.

docs.title: Sample interpolators
docs.text:
The sample_interpolator_t enum in sample_interpolator.h lists the interpolators:

  • constant: between a sample and the next sample, the output is the value of the first sample. Use it for a step, for example a visibility flag or a material index.
  • linear: the output is lerp(value0, value1, alpha). This is the behavior of a track that does not have extended samples.

ACL does not support curves (Bezier, Hermite, Catmull-Rom) at this time.

docs.title: Create an extended track
docs.text:
An extended track type has the _ex suffix: track_float1f_ex to track_vector4f_ex. An extended track list has the same suffix: track_array_float1f_ex to track_array_vector4f_ex. Each sample is a track_extended_sample_t<T> (see track_extended_sample.h) that holds an interpolator and a value. The default interpolator is linear.

Each track in a track list must use the same track interpolator: all the tracks are linear, or all the tracks are extended. In an extended track list, each track can use a different interpolator for each sample.

#include <acl/compression/track_array.h>

using namespace acl;

track_desc_scalarf desc;
desc.output_index = 0;
desc.precision = 0.001F;

track_float1f_ex raw_track = track_float1f_ex::make_reserve(desc, allocator, num_samples, sample_rate);
raw_track[0].set_constant(1.0F);    // Between sample 0 and 1, the value is 1.0
raw_track[1].set_constant(5.0F);    // Between sample 1 and 2, the value is 5.0
raw_track[2].set_linear(2.0F);      // Between sample 2 and 3, the value goes from 2.0 to 8.0
raw_track[3].set_linear(8.0F);
// ...

track_array_float1f_ex raw_track_list(allocator, num_tracks);
raw_track_list[0] = std::move(raw_track);

The raw track list samples extended tracks with the same rules as the compressed tracks. Thus track_array::sample_tracks(..) and track_array::sample_track(..) give the reference values.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
The interpolator of the last sample has an effect only with the wrap policy:

  • With the clamp policy and the non-looping policy, no interval follows the last sample. Thus its interpolator has no effect.
  • With the wrap policy, the interpolator of the last sample controls the interval from the last sample to the first sample.

When compression optimizes a loop (compression_settings::optimize_loops), it removes the last sample because that sample matches the first sample. See how to handle looping playback.

docs.title: Rounding policies
docs.text:
The sample_rounding_policy applies first. Then a constant sample rounds the interpolation alpha down to 0.0. Between a constant sample and the next sample, the output is:

  • none: the value of the constant sample.
  • floor: the value of the constant sample.
  • ceil: the value of the next sample.
  • nearest: the value of the nearest sample.

Thus a constant sample changes only the output of the none policy. With the other policies, a constant sample and a linear sample give the same output. This also applies to each track when you use per_track (see handling per track rounding).

docs.title: Pre-process
docs.text: pre_process_track_list(..) supports extended tracks. It changes only the sample values. The interpolators do not change. See pre-processing raw tracks.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
Use compress_track_list(..) as you do with linear tracks (see compressing raw tracks). Compression measures the error on each sample value. Between two samples, the output is one of the two values or a linear interpolation of them. Thus the track precision also applies between the samples.

The metadata of each track stores one of three modes:

  • linear: each sample is linear.
  • constant: each sample is constant.
  • mixed: the track uses the two interpolators.

Only a mixed track stores the interpolators, with 1 bit for each sample. A constant track (one value for all the samples) stores no interpolator. Thus an extended track where all the samples use the same interpolator has the same size as a linear track.

To select the mode, compression ignores each interpolator that has no effect on the output:

  • The interpolator of the last sample, when the track list does not wrap. No interval follows the last sample.
  • The interpolator of a sample that has the same value as the next sample (binary equality). Each interpolator gives that value.

For example, a track where each sample is constant except the last sample uses the constant mode, and it stores no interpolator. In a track with the linear mode, a constant sample with the same value as the next sample interpolates linearly. Then the output can be 1 ulp from the sample value. This occurs on x86 without FMA, because RTM uses the stable form of the linear interpolation. A linear track with two equal samples has the same behavior.

The compressed tracks use the version v02_02_99_0 (see compressed_tracks_version.h). ACL 2.1 and earlier cannot decompress this data.

docs.title: Decompression
docs.text:
The decompression setting are_extended_samples_supported() controls the code that reads the interpolators (see decompression_settings.h). It is true in all the default decompression settings. If your data has no extended samples, set it to false in your decompression settings. Then the optimizer removes that code.

When the setting is false, decompression_context::initialize(..) returns false for compressed tracks that have extended samples. If skip_initialize_safety_checks() is true, the context does not do this check. Do not decompress extended samples with such a context, because the output is not correct.

The track_writer receives only the output values. The decompression API does not change. See decompressing tracks.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
convert_track_list(..) converts compressed tracks that have extended samples into an extended raw track list. With the scalarf_full scalar format, the conversion also keeps the exact values.

A mixed track keeps the interpolator of each sample. A linear track or a constant track gives the interpolator of its mode to each sample, thus an interpolator that has no effect can change. When each track uses the linear mode, the compressed tracks have no extended samples, and the conversion gives a linear raw track list.

docs.title: The ACL file format
docs.text:
In an .acl.sjson file, an extended track sets interpolator = "extended". Each sample then holds an interpolator and a value:

tracks = [
    {
        name = "step"
        type = "float1f"
        interpolator = "extended"
        precision = 0.001
        output_index = 0
        data = [
            {
                interpolator = "constant"
                value = [ 1.0 ]
            }
            {
                interpolator = "linear"
                value = [ 2.0 ]
            }
        ]
    }
]

A track without an interpolator key is a linear track. See the ACL file format.

docs.title: Data and method used
docs.text:
To compile these statistics, the Matinee fight scene is used.

  • Number of clips: 5
  • Sample rate: 30 FPS
  • Cinematic duration: 66 seconds
  • Troopers 1-4 have 71 bones and the Main Trooper has 551 bones
  • Raw size: 62.38 MB (10x float32 * num bones * num samples)

ACL supports various compression methods but only the overall best variant will be tracked here (see get_default_compression_settings() for details).

The error is measured 3cm away from each bone to simulate the visual mesh skinning process as described here with the default error threshold of 0.01cm. The 99th percentile and the number of samples below the error threshold are calculated by measuring the error on every bone at every sample.
